newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian wage enterprise deals.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian wage enterprise deals.

text.p: Australian federal wage agreements in the December quarter showed an average annualised wage rise of 4.4 percent per employee, down from 4.8 percent in the September quarter, the Department of Industrial Relations said.
For all current federal wage agreements at the end of 1996 the average annualised rise was 4.6 percent per employee, unchanged from the end of September 1996.
Private sector federal agreements formalised in the December quarter showed an average annualised rise of 4.4 percent, down from 5.3 percent in the September quarter.
For all current private sector agreements at the end of December, the average annualised rise was 4.8 percent, unchanged from the end of September.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"A number of 4.5 to 5.0 percent would have been seen as broadly neutral for markets, and we've probably got a result that's slightly on the better end of that range, so it would give the Reserve Bank a little bit more comfort. Five percent would be regarded by the Reserve Bank as excessive, below five percent starts to be more comfortable. I think they wouldn't be completely comforted by these figures, but certainly moving in the right direction. They want to see the outcome of the "living wage" claim, and of course how the economy is performing itself and what pressures that might bring to bear on the labour market later in 1997."

"The December quarter data are a marginal positive for the bond market. You have to remember this series covers only a small percentage of the workforce and many of the deals in this quarter were in weak sectors like retailing. There are enterprise deals coming up in stronger sectors which are much more important. It doesn't change our view on monetary policy which is that the chance of another official cut is very low."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"It's come back a little bit further which is helpful. But I noticed Reith's comments that there were one or two deals in the retail sector in particular that held the pace back, but several other industries are showing quite strong rates of pay increases. So it appears that his department is by no way convinced that wages are benign. I think the RBA will still be fairly cautious. There's nothing there that will really convince them one way or another that they are out of the woods on wages."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"To me this is quite an encouraging sign that wage growth is coming back, certainly into areas where the Reserve Bank will be less worried. I don't think any central bank, and especially the Reserve Bank, will ever say they're not worried about wages growth, and certainly they're not going to become complacent at all, but this I think is just a sign at this stage that wages pressures look to be under control, certainly look to be very consistent with continuing 2-3 percent core inflation."
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"After the last three quarters, from 6.1 percent to 4.4 percent, it is an enormous relief. It's possibly giving us a good signal for tomorrow's figures (final average weekly ordinary time earnings for the November quarter). This is definitely not rate cut material, but it removes the bearishness of the last couple of days in the bond market."
